newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Rate rise, PSBR struggle under UK Labour.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Rate rise, PSBR struggle under UK Labour.

text.p: A Labour government after the next UK general election would raise interest rates promptly but modestly to establish its credibility as inflation picks up, but would struggle to control public spending, a Reuters poll of economic forecasts showed on Tuesday.

Whoever wins the vote due to be held by May 1997 -- opinion polls and economists widely predict it will be Tony Blair's Labour opposition -- will inherit a healthy economy boosted by growing consumer confidence, historically low inflation and falling unemployment after 17 years of Conservative rule.
"There's a very strong probability it will be a Labour government," said James McKay, economist at PaineWebber. "They will inherit quite a strong economy."

The poll, which included independent forecasts from 32 banks, think-tanks and universities, predicted the new administration would act swiftly to raise interest rates, but said the move would not be sharp by the standards of the last few years. Rates were up to 15 percent in 1989, and still double-digit in 1992 before falling to a low of 5.25 in 1994.

The average of 11 base rate forecasts in the poll, which looked ahead to the end of September 1998, predicted they would stand at 6.60 percent by then, less than one percentage point above the current 5.75 percent.

A rise in interest rates under Labour is seen as almost inevitable after months of tension between the UK Treasury and the Bank of England over the appropriate level of borrowing rates. Economists widely believe Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has held base rates down to help a consumer recovery for political reasons, against the bank's advice.
With this in mind, a handful of economists believe Labour's immediate monetary tightening could take rates to seven percent or above.

"They'll inherit a consumer boom that has been stoked up by the Chancellor, erring policy on the side of ease, partly with the election in mind," said Alex Garrard of UBS. "We think they'll need to raise rates higher and more aggressively than they otherwise would have done because of the timing of the election in the economic cycle."
Economists are divided over the extent to which economic recovery has filtered through to consumer spending, creating greater consumer optimism and risking inflation.

"Optimists on inflation argue that falling producer price inflation still has to feed through to the retail level," said John Young at Sanwa Bank. "But I think we are seeing a return of the "feel-good' factor...that may well be recorded in higher retail price inflation (RPIX) soon." August RPIX was 2.8 percent year-on-year and it has been stuck there for four months.

Sanwa's forecast of 3.3 percent inflation in retail prices less mortgage interest payments was the highest in the survey for 1997, compared to a mean average from 30 forecasts of 2.7 percent for the election year.

"Labour is trying to sell itself as the party of financial stability," Young said. "If they did face an environment of rising inflation and didn't do something about it in the first part of their parliamentary term, their credibility in the markets would diminish pretty quickly."

Predictions for GDP growth in the survey pointed to a peak of 3.5 percent around election time in Quarter Two. For the whole of 1997 the average prediction is 3.3 percent annual growth, slightly above the government's own forecast of 3.25 percent for the year.

James McKay at PaineWebber, one of the most bullish on growth with a forecast of 3.8 percent for next year as a whole, noted like several others that this was a consequence of the economic cycle rather than politics.

"My growth forecast is purely based on the dynamics currently evident in the economy. They (Labour) would still face a problem with the PSBR (Public Sector Borrowing Requirement) and steadily rising inflation," McKay noted.
Many economists see few major differences on macro-economic policy between Labour and the Conservatives, predicting a broad continuation of current policies regardless of who is in power.

"Central government departments are already overspending, as you'd expect in the run-up to a general election, but with public sector pay bodies queuing up for payouts under a Labour government I think there's very little reason to expect spending to come under control," said Garrard at UBS.
The poll predicted a PSBR of 27.9 billion stg in 1996/97 and 24.5 billion the following year, modestly overshooting the current official forecasts of 27.0 billion and 23 billion for the two years.
